content:
Workshop 6
 
 # Solving Problems with the Public
 
 Speakers: [Karin Juhl](https:/www.linkedin.com/in/karin-juhl-65b9696/?originalSubdomain=dk) (Development Consultants, Hillerød Kommune, Denmark), [Aline Muylaert](https:/www.linkedin.com/in/alinemuylaert/?originalSubdomain=be) (Co-Founder & Regional Director Benelux, Go Vocal)
 
 This workshop paired a platform demonstration with a practitioner case study. Aline Muylaert, co-founder of Go Vocal, presented the company's digital participation tools and philosophy; Karin Juhl shared how Hillerød Municipality in Denmark has used the platform since 2020. The session offered a window into European civic engagement practices, where statutory requirements for public consultation are stronger than in the U.S.
 
 ## Go Vocal platform and philosophy
 
 [Go Vocal, formerly known as CitizenLab,](https:/www.govocal.com) is a Belgian civic technology company that has worked with over 600 governments and engaged more than two million people across Europe, the U.S., and beyond. Their client list includes capital cities like Oslo, Copenhagen, and Vienna, as well as American cities such as Kansas City, St. Louis, and Salt Lake City. The company rebranded two years ago and was recently ranked a top digital participation platform by [](https:/www.peoplepowered.org) [People Powered](https:/www.peoplepowered.org) , an organization that conducts [global comparisons of participation tools.](https:/www.peoplepowered.org/platform-ratings)
 
 Muylaert framed Go Vocal's mission around three principles: making community engagement more inclusive, more continuous, and more strategic. The platform aims to address what she called "siloed participation," a common problem in local government where fragmented tools and inefficient processes across departments lead to transactional, one-off engagement rather than sustained relationships with residents.
 
 The platform is structured around the [](https:/www.iap2.org/page/pillars) [IAP2 spectrum of participation](https:/www.iap2.org/page/pillars) , ranging from informing residents at the lowest level to empowering them with decision-making authority at the highest. Go Vocal offers tools at each level: surveys for consultation, ideation features for generating proposals, prioritization tools for ranking options, and participatory budgeting and deliberative features for decisions that give communities real power over outcomes.
 
 Several of Go Vocal’s features are intentionally designed to broaden participation. Language accessibility allows residents to engage in their preferred language. Offline integration means paper forms can be scanned through OCR technology and incorporated into the same dataset as online responses. Voice-based participation through speech-to-text enables input from in-person meetings to flow into the digital record. If applicable, the platform also provides demographic dashboards that show administrators how representative their input is by age and other factors, helping them identify gaps and target outreach accordingly.
 
 Go Vocal's AI features focus on processing large volumes of input. The system auto-tags contributions by topic and sentiment, clusters similar responses, and generates summaries. Administrators can also ask questions of the data through a conversational interface built on top of generative AI models. Muylaert emphasized that Go Vocal does not build its own models but layers tools on top of existing LLMs to help users interact with the input they have collected.
 
 ## St. Louis participatory budgeting
 
 [Muylaert described a participatory budgeting project in St. Louis](https:/www.govocal.com/case-studies/st-louis-collects-ideas-from-7000-residents-online) involving $250 million from a legal settlement stemming from the Rams football team's relocation. The city council could not agree on how to spend the funds, so they turned to public engagement. Residents first submitted ideas, which were then clustered into priority categories. The community then voted on these priorities. The top result was investment in water infrastructure, an outcome that surprised the council, who had expected different priorities. This example illustrates how crowdsourcing can surface community preferences that do not match official assumptions.
 
 ## 
 
 ## Hillerød: Five years with Go Vocal and a culture of engagement
 
 Karin Juhl has worked in the Hillerød Municipality for nearly 30 years, focusing on community engagement throughout. Hillerød is a relatively affluent area north of Copenhagen with a well-educated population and expanding development. The municipality began using Go Vocal in 2020 after a four-year process in which a joint committee of politicians and citizens explored ways to improve public engagement. They have since run approximately 50 projects on the platform and registered 4,510 users, roughly 8% of the total population including children.
 
 Hillerød's largest engagement project addressed traffic congestion, a problem Juhl described with local color: residents joke that it is easier to cross Manhattan than to get through Hillerød. The town has gained 5,000 new commuter vehicles over five years as companies have moved to the area, and the historic castle at the center occupies one-fourth of the town, leaving limited space for road expansion.
 
 The engagement process used multiple Go Vocal tools and supplemented digital participation with in-person meetings. The project gathered over 1,400 contributions.
 
 According to Juhl, the outcome surprised politicians: residents clearly stated that the solution was not more roads but more cycling and better public transit. This finding has shifted the policy conversation toward behavior change rather than infrastructure expansion, and Go Vocal will continue to play a role as the municipality explores how to communicate with residents about changing transportation habits.
 
 Hillerød also operates a citizen proposal system. Any resident can submit a proposal, and if it receives at least 450 votes within six months, the mayor and local government are obligated to hold a formal debate on the issue. This does not mean the government must implement the proposal, but it guarantees serious consideration. Even proposals that do not reach the threshold receive attention from Juhl, who routes them to the relevant department to check whether any related work is underway. This proactive follow-up, she argued, helps residents feel that their input matters even when it does not trigger formal action.
 
 ## AI in practice
 
 Juhl offered practical observations on using the AI sense-making features.
 
 The auto-tagging allowed her team to see what topics residents were actually discussing rather than what staff assumed they would discuss. For projects with many open responses across multiple engagement methods, manual analysis would have been prohibitively time-consuming for a small team.
 
 At the same time, she stressed the importance of human verification. Staff check AI-generated summaries against the original contributions to ensure the system is not hallucinating or misrepresenting input. The platform's design allows administrators to trace summaries back to source material, which Juhl identified as essential for maintaining trust in the output.
 
 Regarding challenges in using digital participation platforms, Juhl identified internal buy-in as the most persistent. Politicians tend to be enthusiastic about public engagement. Frontline staff who work directly with residents are often receptive as well. The resistance typically comes from middle management, where workloads are heavy and the unpredictability of public input can complicate planning. Engagement introduces what Juhl called a "dark horse" into decision-making: resident opinions sometimes lead politicians to change direction, which can create tension with managers who prefer clearer paths forward.
 
 To address this, Juhl monitors the municipality's annual development plans and budget documents to identify projects where engagement could add value, then approaches the relevant staff directly. Training happens just-in-time rather than in advance. She emphasized that the platform is intuitive enough that younger colleagues pick it up quickly, but engagement must be relevant and imminent for training to stick.
 
 She also noted that cross-departmental project groups produce better engagement designs because they bring diverse channels for reaching residents rather than relying on a single outreach strategy.
 
 ## Key takeaways for course development
 
 ## 
 
 Digital participation tools can consolidate fragmented tools and participation methods into a single system, allowing staff across departments and methods to access the same data and reducing duplication of effort.
 
 AI sense-making features are most valuable for processing large volumes of open-ended text, but require human verification and traceability to source material to maintain credibility.
 
 The IAP2 spectrum provides a useful framework for matching tools to the level of influence being offered to residents, from informing through empowering.
 
 Citizen proposal systems with clear thresholds for formal response create accountability without requiring governments to implement every suggestion.
 
 Public engagement can surface community priorities that differ from official assumptions, as demonstrated by both the St. Louis and Hillerød cases.
 
 Blending online and offline methods, including paper forms and in-person meetings, broadens reach and improves representativeness.
 
 ## 
 
 ## Audience notes
 
 Questions
 
 “How do you increase engagement and access for underrepresented groups?”
 
 “How do decision-makers explain what we heard and what we couldn't do?”
 
 “Do different decision-makers need different summarization formats from AI tools?”
 
 “Have partners built incentive structures to support full engagement?”
 
 “How do you get enough participants, how long should engagement run, and how do you account for bias when certain populations cannot participate?”
 
 “How do you ensure contributions are genuine and not from bots or special interests?”
 
 “Has technology changed how much should be budgeted for outreach and awareness-raising?”
 
 ## Quotes
 
 ### Aline Mulyaert (Go Vocal)
 
 “Community engagement can be more inclusive, continuous, and strategic… so that in the end, we build more trust in our governments, in our democracy.”
 
 “Governments are facing siloed participation. They have lots of fragmented tools, inefficient processes across teams, across departments, and that often leads to reduced and transactional engagements.”
 
 “Platforms are nice, tools are nice, technology is nice, but eventually it comes down to the people working with these technologies within the government.”
 
 ### Karin Juhl (Hillerød Kommune)
 
 “What is fantastic about AI sense-making is that we can ask open questions, so we don’t have to kind of guess what is this about for the citizens… We easily get into the tradition about thinking we know what this question is about, and then we ask from our logic all the questions.”
 
 “We have to check up that it’s actually not hallucinating anything or getting things wrong… We have this fantastic thing where we can get into the original data and see, is it actually a sensible resume that it is making.”
 
 “If we had to work with this in a traditional way, it would have taken all too many resources. We are not so many people that work with this.”
